title: Black DJs playing black records; Elvis, the Beatles and rock and roll
summary: Asked how Winslow felt coaching Duke Thiel, Tex describes college-trained black DJs breaking into radio and how race records became rock and roll.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: Did Vernon ever talk about how he, how did he feel when he was coaching Duke Field? I mean, what was his feeling about having Duke Field?

Well, he, well, you see, he didn't like it, but he was trying to make a point to let people know that blacks were qualified to do just about any damn thing. I think that was a period in time that people like myself, or Ebron Jay, who was known as Ernest the Whip, and Malcolm Laplaz, who is now, Dr. Malcolm Laplaz, who now lives in California. We were trying to prove to the city of New Orleans and the listeners that some of us were college-trained people who could open a new era of communication on these radio stations so that we could compete or do just as well as whites. And a lot of people started accepting us for that. Because you've got to remember that a lot of the disc jockeys who were on the air at that time, they would not pick up a black record. Or if they did play a Duke Ellington or a Count Faces record, it was a race record. But now with Duke Field coming on the air, then with Dr. Daddio, and then with Planet of the Whip, and then with myself started strictly playing black records, then we start losing these disc jockeys because we were in other words, the blacks started listening to us. And here's where the explosion came. All of a sudden, here comes Elvis Presley. Wow! Boy! But you see, Elvis told the story that he was emulating whites, the way they danced, the way they played music. Then, along two years after Elvis, here comes the Beatles from England. Well, the whites got it back again. They held it for a little while. But then all of a sudden, with the coming of integration, blacks and whites started recording together, and you know, like the, like Aaron Neville and the other lady, the other lady records with. Oh, Linda Ronstad. Linda Ronstad. Linda Ronstad. Things started fully beginning to change. Then you had people like Alan Toussaint, who came on the, the being who started directing the Beatles, at least. He didn't direct the whole Beatles structure, but he also, I'm trying to think, one of the Beatles. Paul McCartney. Paul McCartney came to New Orleans. Right. And he recorded right there in the studio that Alan Toussaint and his business partners own today. So things were slowly beginning to change. And eventually, it was no longer race records. It became, with Elvis Presley and the Beatles and the other black contributors, it became rock and roll. That's what it was. It became rock and roll. That's what it was. It became rock and roll.
